Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
733 AM EDT Thu Aug 27 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 230 AM EDT Thursday...

Strong to possibly severe thunderstorm chances this afternoon
have increased across southwestern Vermont. A Slight Risk has 
been introduced to Essex County, NY and Addison and Rutland 
Counties in Vermont for this afternoon. There is also increasing
confidence in potential localized flash flooding across Rutland
County and southern Vermont this afternoon/evening from 
potential training thunderstorms.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 230 AM EDT Thursday...

1. Thunderstorms are likely this afternoon and evening, with 
greater chances in Vermont and particularly in our southern areas. 
Some storms will be capable of strong winds, small hail, and heavy 
rain. 

2. Some lingering showers will be possible early on Friday, 
before high pressure, and drying conditions lead to a quiet weekend.

3. An active weather pattern will prevail early next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 230 AM EDT Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Confidence in afternoon showers and thunderstorms, some 
of which could be strong to severe, remains on track. SPC has nudged 
the Slight Risk (level 2 out of 5) for severe thunderstorms 
northeast to include Essex County NY, and Rutland and Addison 
Counties in Vermont for this afternoon. The areas included in the 
previous Marginal Risk for severe thunderstorms for today has 
remained unchanged. Synoptically, an occluding surface low with 
associated warm front over western New York this morning will lift 
through the region early to mid this afternoon. Showers will be 
possible along the warm front as early as mid to late this morning 
along the southern Greens and St. Lawrence Valley. Water vapor 
depictions upstream into western New York and Pennsylvania show 
decent dry air ahead of a stout boundary of showers in western 
Pennsylvania. This clearing will help our region destabilize this 
afternoon as MLCAPE surges to 1000-1500J/kg, with some pockets of 
1500-2000J/kg across the eastern Adirondacks and Champlain Valley. 
While there will be good instability in the warm sector this 
afternoon as temperatures climb to near 80, with dewpoints in the 
low 60s, deep layer shear will be less than ideal for strong 
organized storms. 20-30knots of bulk 0-6km shear is expected this 
afternoon, which is on the lower side of sufficient shear for severe 
storms; the better shear will be well to our east near the main cold 
front. Regardless, numerous showers and scattered thunderstorms, 
with some isolated storms becoming strong to severe, are 
anticipated, mainly in the 3-8 PM timeframe, moving west to east.

The main risks associated with our storm potential this afternoon 
will be gusty winds, isolated small hail. Although shear is on the 
lower bounds for favorable severe conditions, storms modes look to 
favor some mini bowing segments and multicells which can drive 
strong cold pools and thus isolated gusty winds. Given decent mid 
level lapse rates to 6-7C/km, and good elevated instability in the 
hail growth zone, small hail will be possible within stronger 
updrafts. While the probabilities are low, there is a low risk for 
some isolated rotation within storms this afternoon. As the warm 
front lifts through the region this afternoon, winds in the low 
level will turn more southeasterly, and paired with prevailing 
southwesterly flow aloft, veering flow could lead to an increase in 
low level spin. 0-1km SRH will be low around 100-150 m2/s2, though 
could be enough to lead to some isolated rotation, especially should 
any storms develop along the warm front, and out ahead of the main 
boundary this afternoon. All hazards will be possible this 
afternoon, though the main concerns will be winds in the form of 
straight-lined winds. At this time, a greater risk/more coverage of 
stronger storms is favored south of our region per consensus of both 
the physically-based and machine learning model guidance.

Heavy rain will also be a concern with WPC placing the entire area 
in a Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) for a 5% chance of exceeding 
flash flood guidance within 25 miles of an area. Pwats will be 
around 1.5-1.7 inches, the 85th percentile for this time of year, 
with modest warm layer cloud depths around 10,000 ft. While these do 
not favor flash flood potential, the flash flood risk today will be 
driven by conditional training storms. Cells may become aligned to 
the background flow across southern Vermont and lead to a localized 
chance for flash flooding. Probabilities for 2" of rain through 8 AM 
Friday highlight western Rutland County in areas like Fair Haven, 
and Rutland itself in a 20% probability. HREF probabilities denote a 
10% chance for this area to see upwards of 3". These high rainfall 
amounts will be highly conditional on training thunderstorms and 
does still appear unlikely, though there is some better confidence 
than previous forecasts for this area to see some localized flash 
flooding. Have increased rainfall amounts to reflect this in 
southern Vermont to around an inch, to locally 1-2" should a few 
thunderstorms move over the same areas. Interests in southern 
Vermont, should pay close attention to our forecast and radar trends 
this afternoon, as conditions could change quickly.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A cold front will gradually move from west to east early 
Friday spurring some lingering showers across Vermont. Given the 
timing of the frontal passage, instability will be low, so 
anticipating just some light showers. Though should the front slow 
as it nears the VT/NH border, some isolated rumbles of thunder may 
be possible. Showers will taper off Friday early to mid afternoon, 
with clearing skies from west to east. Temperatures will be a few 
degrees cooler than Thursday in the low to mid 70s, with perhaps 
some upper 70s, should the cold front slow as it moves east allowing 
for more diurnal heating in the deeper valleys. Lows Friday night 
will cool off under strong radiational cooling into the upper 40s 
for most locations, outside of areas near the St. Lawrence River and 
Lake Champlain where low 50s are expected. Some pocket low 40s, to 
near 40 will be possible in the more sheltered locations of the 
Adirondacks. With the strong radiational cooling, valley fog 
following the recent rains will be possible. Saturday looks to be 
pleasant with temperatures in the mid to upper 70s under high 
pressure. Some light southwest channeled flow in the St. Lawrence 
Valley will be possible, though by and large winds will remain light 
under 10 MPH. Clouds will increase Saturday night.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Sunday into Monday, a vigorous vort will dig towards the 
base of a longwave trough pattern positioned in Quebec Province. 
Meanwhile, a strong upper high in the Desert Southwest will weaken 
and shift east. This will open up a stream of tropical Pacific air 
that tracks along the international border. This will result in 
accelerating flow over our region with systems. Surface high 
pressure will build across Quebec Province once the vigorous vort 
pushes east. The northeasterly flow from that high and the attempt 
for warm, humid air eking closer to us will place us near along a 
stationary moisture gradient through at least next Wednesday.

There's plenty of spread, but perusing various ensemble 
probabilities of greater than 0.5" shows some potential throughout 
Monday through Thursday. Taking in a view of a 72-hour time frame, 
NBM probabilities for at least 2" in the Monday-Thursday time frame 
is about 10-15% and 30-40% for an inch of rain. So a period of above 
normal precipitation appears likely heading into next week. Will 
fine tune the timing as we draw a little closer. Temperatures will 
be run relatively close to seasonal norms (mid to upper 70s at day, 
50s at night, but 40s for the Adirondack Regional Airport).

&&

.AVIATION /12Z THURSDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Through 12Z Friday...Conditions are mainly VFR. Despite VADs
indicating model forecast winds off the surface likely verified
with KCXX noting 20 knots at 1000 feet, KMPV still managed to 
observe prevailing LIFR ceilings and visibility due to fog. 
Upstream, scattered showers are approaching the area. It's 
possible they produce rain at KMPV/KRUT/KEFK as they lift 
northeast. The primary batch of showers and storms will come 
from a boundary on the eastern half of Lake Ontario. Ahead of 
the feature, south winds will increase to 8-14 knots sustained 
with gusts 17-24 knots, with the highest speeds at 
KBTV/KPBG/KMSS. Storms will be more hit or miss across northern 
New York from about 16z-21z, but activity appears more likely to
coalesce near KRUT and noted prevailing TSRA from 23z-04z as 
the boundary appears to briefly stall over that region. Heavy 
rain and gusty winds could occur in thunderstorms, and will be 
most likely at KRUT. Winds will trend light and variable for 
most, and as clouds clear, fog will likely develop as early as 
02-04z.

Outlook...

Friday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Scattered SHRA.
Friday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Saturday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Saturday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Sunday: VFR. Chance SHRA.
Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Monday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight chance SHRA.

&&

.MARINE...
As of 230 AM EDT Thursday...

A Lake Wind Advisory is in effect for the broad and northern waters 
of Lake Champlain until 8 PM today. South winds ahead an approaching 
frontal system will lead to increasing channeled winds on Lake 
Champlain by late this morning enhancing gusts and wave 
conditions. Winds and gusts on the lake will increase to 15 to 
25 knots through this afternoon. Waves will be generally 1 to 3 
ft. Gusts will weaken back to around 10 to 15 knots after sunset
this evening with the passage of a boundary. Thunderstorms will
be possible this afternoon primarily between 2-6 PM, which can 
further enhance gusty winds. Within any thunderstorms, small 
hail, and heavy rain will also be possible.

&&

.BTV WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
VT...None.
NY...None.

&&

$$
